item.title: CoreWeave bond rout tests market's math on AI buildout
item.description: A sharp decline in CoreWeave's bonds this week is emerging as a test of investors' willingness to keep financing the massive buildout of AI infrastructure, as rising borrowing costs and scrutiny of debt-funded expansion hit the sector.
item.dc:creator: Suzanne McGee, Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss
item.content:encoded: A sharp decline in CoreWeave's (CRWV.O) bonds this week is emerging as a test of investors' willingness to keep financing the massive buildout of AI infrastructure, as rising borrowing costs and scrutiny of debt-funded expansion hit the sector. Analysts and portfolio managers said the selloff in the data center operator's debt carries more significance than a concurrent rout in its shares because it may signal a broader reassessment of the risks tied to financing AI projects that may take years to generate revenue. CoreWeave bonds issued in June at a yield of 9.675% have plunged in value, sending their yield to 15% this week. "CoreWeave is absolutely the canary in the coal mine" for a market segment that is coming under more stress, said Max Frumes, global head of distressed and leveraged finance at 9fin, a fintech corporate credit data and analytics company. "This is going to be a turning point in the pricing and availability and structure of credit that's supporting the AI boom," said Frumes, who believes that other AI-linked debt will follow CoreWeave into distressed territory. "It's going to get more expensive. There will be a lot more scrutiny and probably some pushback from investors." CoreWeave shares fell 15.1% from Monday's open through Thursday's close, despite a 6% gain on Thursday after a [USN:L4N46112V TEXT:"vote of confidence from partner Nvidia NVDA.O"]. The decline was broadly in line with weakness in other so-called neocloud companies such as Nebius (NBIS.O) and Iren (IREN.O) . Credit investors said they already are [USN:L6N45611M TEXT:"becoming more selective"]. "We're definitely taking another look at our exposures across the AI infrastructure space, particularly where the risks are concentrated and whether we're being adequately compensated for taking them," said John Han, a portfolio manager at fixed-income asset management firm F/m Investments. F/m's portfolio contains unsecured CoreWeave bonds in one of its exchange-traded funds, but only because they make up part of the index tracked by the ETF. At their current yields those bonds "certainly deserve another look," Han said. He generally prefers to invest in high-yield securities via special purpose vehicles that may offer lower yields but also more collateral and less risk. "The market is being very selective and really singling out anything that has more leverage, and (that may be) in a bit more challenging operating environment," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager of fixed income at Catalyst funds. To Holzenthaler and other investors, what the markets are witnessing now is an overreaction as sentiment shifts from being overly upbeat to downright bearish. In June, the risks driving the selloff -- the sheer size of the funding needs, the leverage, the reliance on outside financing, the risk that the GPUs (graphics processing units) being purchased for data centers would be obsolete before the new facilities could open -- were merely overlooked or downplayed. "A few months ago, I would have said people were just too optimistic around AI," Holzenthaler said. Deutsche Bank global head of macro and thematic research Jim Reid sees the market entering a new phase in which debt financing is becoming increasingly important. "As we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Reid wrote in a recent report. "AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges." Vanguard bond portfolio manager Brad Collins said assessing AI-related debt has become more challenging as issuers bring increasingly large and varied offerings to market, often forcing investors to make decisions in days or even hours. Rising inflation has pushed financing costs higher overall and fueled concern about what lies ahead for mammoth AI capital spending plans. Then there is the [USN:L6N43G12P TEXT:"growing political controversy"] surrounding the construction of data centers. Even one of the tech sector's stalwarts allows that the road ahead may be bumpy at times. Dan Ives, partner and technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, an investment firm, estimates that 5% to 10% of planned projects ultimately will not be built. "The growing noise around data center permitting and midterm rhetoric on power prices has given investors another reason to step back," Ives said.

item.title: US holds more secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
item.description: The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Poppy McPherson, John Geddie
item.content:encoded: The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup. Earlier talks in Myanmar's capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously [USN:L6N45T16N TEXT:"reported"]. It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week's talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting. US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar. The US State Department declined to comment on Vance's presence in the delegation but said the bureau he heads was not playing a leading role on US policy toward Myanmar. The department's Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs is "shaping, implementing and engaging on" US policy toward the country, a spokesperson said, while Vance's Bureau of Intelligence and Research "informs policy makers but does not lead on policy." "The United States does not comment on the content and parameters of purported sensitive discussions," the spokesperson said, adding that the engagement with Myanmar "is rooted in the desire to achieve practical wins for the American people — particularly those impacted by transnational crime." A spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges. Last month's meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar's coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going. A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar's help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said. Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar's leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar's military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres. US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar's large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role. The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country. "This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move. Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington [USN:S0N2TK07R TEXT:"declared a genocide"]. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says. The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank. "The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said. JAPAN'S ROLE UNCLEAR It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar. Japan's acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar's military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration. That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper. Japan's Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe's trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government. Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained. Japan condemned the military's 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities. Tokyo was one of Myanmar's largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China's influence in one of Asia's last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup. Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan's trade promotion agency, JETRO.

item.title: Indonesia gets 'wake-up call' as MSCI prepares to expel it from global indexes
item.description: Indonesia's stock market is no longer worthy of "emerging market" status, MSCI said on Friday, laying out a plan to remove it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998.
item.dc:creator: Stefanno Sulaiman, Ankur Banerjee
item.content:encoded: Indonesia's stock market is no longer worthy of "emerging market" status, MSCI said on Friday, laying out a plan to remove it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998. Coming a month ahead of a scheduled review, MSCI's change of tack [USN:L1N46203P TEXT:"stunned investors"] and irked Jakarta officials, with the Indonesian regulator unveiling sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms. The benchmark stock index (.JKSE) , already the world's [USN:L4N43G12X TEXT:"worst performer"] this year, closed down 11.57%, in its biggest single-day drop since January 1998. The rupiah currency slid as much as 0.8% to 18,070 a dollar, its weakest since late July, but recovered some ground. Equities in Southeast Asia's biggest economy have struggled since a January freeze in the MSCI indexes, with a [USN:L6N46202Y TEXT:"threatened downgrade"] to "frontier" status because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour. The market has lost more than $350 billion in capitalisation since, with about $60 billion wiped out on Friday alone. MSCI cited insufficient reforms to tackle the problems and said even a downgrade to "frontier" status would not reflect the severity of the issues, but proposed instead to move further beyond that, to [USN:L6N46208E TEXT:""standalone" status"]. "Significant concerns remain around market dysfunction," MSCI said in a statement on Friday. "Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia's continued classification as an emerging market no longer appropriate." The lower "standalone" status it proposed would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by billions of dollars in passive investment, forcing funds that follow, or are ranked against, the indexes, to sell. UBS estimated such a move could trigger about $4 billion of passive outflows from Indonesia, with active investors potentially adding a further $15 billion in outflow. Foreign investors have already net sold $4.7 billion worth of Indonesian stocks in 2026. Indonesia's senior economic minister, Airlangga Hartarto, said there was "a big question mark" over why MSCI did not discuss the downgrade to "standalone" status during a meeting this week in the Thai capital of Bangkok. He made the comment ahead of a meeting of top officials, including the finance minister, the governor of the central bank and other related officials to discuss MSCI's announcement. The Indonesia Stock Exchange said it had taken concrete steps to enhance transparency and integrity in the capital market, and CEO Jeffrey Hendrik said he would request further clarification on the basis of the announcement. The move did not reflect the health of the vast majority of listed companies or indeed the Indonesian economy, said Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, adding that "grouping Indonesia with Lebanon, Palestine, and Argentina does not make sense". He added, "This is a wake-up call for Indonesia." Indonesia would be the largest economy in the group if it was downgraded to "standalone" status. MSCI SCRUTINY RAISES MORE QUESTIONS MSCI's announcement piles pressure on the government of President Prabowo Subianto. It is the latest of a series of setbacks for Indonesia this year, with [USN:L4N3Z114D TEXT:"Moody's"] and [USN:L1N3ZS06T TEXT:"Fitch"] cutting their sovereign rating outlooks to negative, citing reduced policymaking credibility. "The proposal highlights MSCI's dissatisfaction with the pace of reforms and raises further questions about the investability of the market," said Tan Altundag, investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management. "The investment implications could be significant," said Altundag, who has no holdings in Indonesia. The office of Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara, who chairs the financial stability board, did not reply to a request for comment. In a sign of investor anxiety over the index provider's move, there was a rush for the exits when the market opened, triggering a 30-minute trading halt on the Jakarta exchange. "It's the first time this has ever happened in my 20 years in the stock market," said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia, referring to the chaotic opening minutes. MSCI's move seemed heavy-handed, given Indonesia's efforts to [USN:L6N42W0D2 TEXT:"tackle issues"] around market transparency and increase the free-float requirement for listed firms, Mackintosh added. "The only way for Indonesia to remedy this situation would be to impose severe sanctions and fines on those involved in concerted share manipulation," he said. After the MSCI move, Indonesia's Financial Services Authority (OJK) disclosed fines of millions of dollars for market participants involved in trading violations concerning three listed firms - Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA.JK) , Barito Renewables Energy (BREN.JK) and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi (CUAN.JK) . Investors allegedly conducted "planned and structured" price manipulation of Dian Swastatika's shares, said Hasan Fawzi, an official of the regulator. Shares offered in the IPOs of Barito Renewables and Petrindo were allegedly intended from the outset for parties linked to the controlling shareholder, leading to concentrated ownership. The companies did not immediately respond to Reuters emails seeking comment. DOWNGRADE PLANNED FOR MID-2027 MSCI said it would run a consultation with market participants for a downgrade to "standalone" status until April 2027 and then proceed with reclassification unless it finds clear evidence of improvement in market governance and function. Standalone markets are not included in MSCI's emerging or frontier index products, which are tracked by passive funds and treated as performance benchmarks for other fund managers. MSCI says reclassification to standalone status may occur in the case of severe deterioration in market accessibility or size and liquidity, with Argentina the most recent example.

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: Chine-La croissance du PIB a accéléré au T3, battant les attentes
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chine-La croissance du PIB a accéléré au T3, battant les attentes PEKIN, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Le produit intérieur brut (PIB) de la Chine a progressé de 4,5% en rythme annuel au troisième trimestre, montrent des données officielles publiées lundi, un rythme supérieur aux attentes des analystes et qui atténue la pression pesant sur Pékin pour qu'il déploie des mesures supplémentaires de stimulus. Wall Street termine en nette baisse, plombée par l'IA et le pétrole La Bourse de New York a fini en nette baisse vendredi, encore une fois plombée par les inquiétudes entourant l'endettement des entreprises du secteur de l'intelligence artificielle, mais aussi par une nouvelle hausse des prix du pétrole.   L'Europe finit dans le vert, la "tech" pénalise à nouveau le Nasdaq Les Bourses européennes ont terminé en hausse vendredi et sur de solides gains hebdomadaires, les indices du Vieux Continent restant largement épargnés par les craintes sur le secteur technologique qui secouent à nouveau Wall Street, et renouent avec un peu de sérénité grâce à la baisse des rendements obligataires. Shell s’accorde avec DCC Energy sur la cession de ses stations-service en France, selon une source Shell a scellé une entente avec DCC Energy, basée à Dublin, pour la vente de son réseau de stations-service et de services connexes en France, selon une source proche du dossier et des documents consultés par Reuters. UniCredit autorisé par la BCE à prendre le contrôle de Commerzbank UniCredit a obtenu l'autorisation de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) pour prendre le contrôle de Commerzbank, a annoncé jeudi soir la banque italienne, alors que son offre publique d'achat hostile a porté sa participation dans son concurrent allemand à 48%. FMI: L'Europe doit stimuler la croissance ou emprunter moins pour garantir la viabilité de sa dette L'Europe doit croître plus rapidement ou emprunter moins pour maintenir sa dette sur une trajectoire viable, a déclaré vendredi le Fonds monétaire international (FMI), soulignant que les plans de redressement prévus pourraient ne pas être suffisants. UBS étudie des options à l'étranger au cas la réglementation suisse devient insupportable à ses yeux selon des sources UBS étudie différents scénarios, dont un déménagement de son siège social ou une fusion avec une autre banque, au cas où la Suisse adopterait de nouvelles règles bancaires que le groupe jugerait excessivement strictes, selon trois sources proches du dossier. Schneider relève ses objectifs 2026 après un T3 record porté par les centres de données Schneider Electric a relevé vendredi pour la deuxième fois de l’année ses objectifs de résultat d'exploitation et de chiffre d’affaires 2026, porté par la demande des géants du cloud pour les centres de données dédiés à l’intelligence artificielle. Christine Lagarde pourrait être nommée présidente du Forum de Davos dès novembre-sources Le Forum économique mondial (WEF) pourrait nommer Christine Lagarde à sa présidence dès novembre, ont déclaré à Reuters quatre sources proches de l'organisation, ce qui impliquerait un départ anticipé de ses fonctions à la tête de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). L’AIE va accélérer la mise sur le marché des stocks de pétrole, dont plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel L’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE) est convenue jeudi de mettre sur le marché plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel dès que possible, ainsi que les volumes restants des réserves d’urgence libérées en mars, afin de contribuer à approvisionner le marché et à freiner la flambée des prix.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Canada-Un feu de prairie sur une base militaire en Alberta tue 4 personnes CALGARY, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Un incendie déclenché par un feu de broussailles a tué quatre soldats et fait 39 blessés, dont 19 se trouvent dans un état critique, sur une base d'entraînement de l'armée canadienne dans la province de l'Alberta, dans l'ouest du pays, ont déclaré dimanche soir les autorités locales. Trump dispose d'un délai pour se prononcer sur les sanctions contre la Russie, dit Rubio 17 octobre (Reuters) - Le secrétaire d'Etat américain Marco Rubio a déclaré samedi que Donald Trump disposait d'un délai pouvant aller jusqu'à 60 jours pour évaluer l'impact économique des sanctions et des droits de douane liés à la Russie. L'Egypte prête à contribuer à la sécurité de l'Arabie saoudite 18 octobre (Reuters) - L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne. Première apparition publique du pape depuis son opération pour un cancer du poumon CITE DU VATICAN, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon. Les USA ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine, dit Zelensky 18 octobre (Reuters) - Les États-Unis ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine pour l'aider à se défendre contre les attaques de missiles russes, a déclaré dimanche le président Volodimir Zelensky. Trump apporte son soutien à Netanyahu pour les élections en Israël WASHINGTON, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a apporté dimanche son soutien à Benjamin Netanyahu en vue des prochaines élections législatives israéliennes. Un ministre russe au FMI boycotté par les Européens Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes. Vaste manifestation à Tunis contre le président Saïed Des milliers de personnes ont manifesté samedi à Tunis contre le président Kaïs Saïed, l'accusant de saper la démocratie et l'économie du pays. Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon. Zelensky dénonce de nouvelles restrictions imposées par Starlink L'Ukraine n'est pas en mesure d'utiliser ses systèmes d'interception contre les attaques de drones russes en raison de restrictions de vitesse imposées par Starlink, a déclaré samedi le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, ajoutant que Kyiv discutait de cette question avec des responsables américains.
